stories.title: South Africa: Cachalia Drops Apartheid Truth Bombs As Latest Stats Show '60 Killed Daily in SA'

The measures include a ban on concerts, festivals and political rallies without clearance from the Ministry of Health, alongside mandatory 21-day quarantine or monitored self-isolation for Ugandans returning from the DRC. The government has also tightened passenger screening at airports, introduced stricter monitoring of hotels and schools, and restricted the movement of humanitarian workers and bodies across its borders. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The restrictions, which took effect immediately, follow concerns over continued movement between Uganda and the DRC, including through unofficial crossing points that could facilitate the spread of the deadly virus. In a public health advisory issued on November 19, Uganda's Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary Diana Atwine said the National Task Force on Epidemic Preparedness and Response had approved the additional interventions following an assessment of the risks posed by the outbreak in the neighbouring DRC. "With the current heightened surveillance, the ministry has observed continued movement of people across our borders, including through ungazetted crossing points, which has increased the risk of the disease entering Uganda and spreading to our communities and to other countries," Atwine said.

stories.summary: Somalia: Somaliland Rejects Somalia's Claim of Authority Over Its Foreign Relations HornDiplomat Somaliland President Dr. Abdirahman Mohamed Abdillahi Irro 19 November 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Mohamed Duale Hargeisa — Somaliland rejected Somalia's claims of jurisdiction over its affairs on Thursday, accusing Mogadishu of trying to speak on its behalf and saying its diplomatic engagements, economic partnerships and strategic arrangements require no approval from Somalia. "The Republic of Somaliland rejects the Somalian Government's claims of jurisdiction over its sovereign affairs," the government said. "Somaliland exercises exclusive authority over its territory and foreign relations." In a press release issued in Hargeisa, Somaliland's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said the dispute followed a series of moves by Somalia's government concerning Somaliland's dealings abroad. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "The Government of the Republic of Somaliland takes note of a series of recent actions by the Somalian Government purporting to speak for or constrain Somaliland's external relations," the ministry said. "These actions carry no authority over Somaliland's sovereign decisions and constitute an unwarranted attempt to interfere in matters beyond Mogadishu's jurisdiction." The ministry pointed to Somaliland's independence from Britain on June 26, 1960, five days before the former Italian-administered territory gained independence and the two territories united. It argued that the union was never duly ratified through a mutually agreed and legally binding Act of Union and that Somaliland's original sovereignty therefore remained intact. "On 18 May 1991, Somaliland restored the exercise of its sovereign authority within the internationally established boundaries inherited at independence, consistent with the African principle of uti possidetis juris," the ministry said. "Somaliland's position is therefore one of restored statehood, not secession." The ministry said Somaliland's national interests guide its foreign policy and that its relationships with international partners are based on mutual respect and shared interests. "Its diplomatic engagements, economic partnerships, and strategic arrangements are founded on mutual respect and shared interests and are not subject to authorization or consent from Mogadishu," the ministry said. "The Government of the Republic of Somaliland underscores that unilateral claims of jurisdiction, regardless of their form, neither confer authority over Somaliland's external affairs nor diminish its right to pursue independent international partnerships." The ministry said Somaliland would continue to pursue international cooperation while safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity. "The Republic of Somaliland remains steadfast in safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity while advancing mutually beneficial international cooperation and contributing to regional peace, stability, and prosperity," it said. A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable. "Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC. "Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up." Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed. Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding. In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district. Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village. "As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes.

stories.title: Africa: Africa Accounts for Half of World's Children Living in Conflict Zones, NGO Warns
stories.summary: Africa Accounts for Half of World's Children Living in Conflict Zones, NGO Warns UNICEF/Ahmed Satti Children walk at a camp for displaced persons in Port Sudan, which is hosting families who fled violence across the country, including Darfur and Kordofan regions. 19 November 2026 Radio France Internationale By RFI Around 260 million children in Africa were living close to armed conflict in 2025 - amounting to two in five, a larger proportion than ever previously recorded, the charity Save the Children said in a report on Thursday. Worldwide, nearly one in four children lived near fighting. The number of children living in conflict zones in Africa rose by nearly 20 percent from 2024 to 2025, when the continent accounted for 44 percent of the global total. Around one in eight lived in conflict zones in 2010, compared with around two in five in 2025 - roughly the same share as in the Middle East . Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Meanwhile, the global count climbed from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025, the highest since records began in 1990.

stories.summary: «Chacun doit mettre la main à la poche»: en Tunisie, des propos de la ministre des Finances font polémique En Tunisie, les ministres passent un à un devant le Parlement et la seconde chambre, le conseil national des districts et des régions, pour présenter les lignes directrices de leur budget respectif pour la loi de finances 2027. stories.title: COP31: la RDC présente sa feuille de route pour lutter contre le réchauffement climatique
stories.summary: COP31: la RDC présente sa feuille de route pour lutter contre le réchauffement climatique Les négociations sont toujours en cours à la COP31. stories.summary: Ghana: le nouveau jet présidentiel suscite la polémique en pleine hausse du coût de la vie Au Ghana, le nouveau jet présidentiel a atterri lundi 16 novembre 2026 à Accra. stories.title: Le Maroc veut investir près de 365 millions d'euros pour développer son industrie de défense
stories.summary: Le Maroc veut investir près de 365 millions d'euros pour développer son industrie de défense Le Maroc veut devenir un acteur qui compte dans l’industrie de l’armement. Il a annoncé mercredi 18 novembre mobiliser 400 millions de dollars pour accélérer le développement du secteur de la défense. Le royaume chérifien mise sur les technologies de pointe comme les drones et l’intelligence artificielle. stories.title: Libye: en recevant le Premier ministre Dbeibah, l’Égypte rééquilibre ses relations avec Tripoli
stories.summary: Libye: en recevant le Premier ministre Dbeibah, l’Égypte rééquilibre ses relations avec Tripoli Cette visite du Premier ministre libyen Abdelhamid Dbeibah en Égypte est décrite à Tripoli comme « la plus importante jamais effectuée par un responsable de l'Ouest libyen » depuis 13 ans. stories.title: Est de la RDC: l'armée congolaise à l'offensive face à des alliés du groupe politico-militaire FRN
stories.summary: Est de la RDC: l'armée congolaise à l'offensive face à des alliés du groupe politico-militaire FRN Dans l'est de la RDC, les affrontements violents se multiplient depuis le début de semaine dans le Sud-Kivu, plus précisément dans les hauts plateaux des territoires d’Uvira et Fizi. stories.title: International Crisis Group recommande des négociations entre les régimes militaires sahéliens et le Jnim
stories.summary: International Crisis Group recommande des négociations entre les régimes militaires sahéliens et le Jnim « La bataille pour les villes : contrer la menace du Jnim sur les centres urbains du Sahel », c'est le titre du rapport publié ce vendredi 20 novembre par International Crisis Group (ICG), organisation non gouvernementale de recherche spécialisée sur la prévention et l'analyse des conflits. stories.summary: Reportage Afrique Madagascar: la région du Bongolava en proie aux feux de brousse Publié le : 20/11/2026 - 00:00 À Madagascar, le mois de novembre est marqué par une multiplication des feux dans les zones rurales, juste avant que ne débutent les pluies, soutenues et quotidiennes. stories.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PevZ Prefer DW on Google 'We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming,' Beatrice Atim Anywar, Uganda's environment minister, told DW Image: DW Advertisement Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change. "This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods." In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production. "When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change. "It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added. In October 2025, landslides triggered by heavy rainfall in Uganda's Kaptang village destroyed people's homes Image: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans. Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

Photograph: Courtesy of CPJ Africa Mentors, colleagues and friends: tributes paid to the ‘Eritrea 16’ who disappeared 25 years ago Families of journalists who vanished into state prisons on ‘Black Tuesday’ in 2001 do not know whether they are even still alive When Fisseha Yirgalem stepped on to the podium and began reading from a letter written to a man who may never hear it, the room full of journalists in Nairobi fell quiet. The Eritrean writer’s personal tribute to Amanuel Asrat , a poet, writer, and founder of Zemen newspaper, was not merely about an abstract human rights case but about her mentor, former colleague and friend whose life had in effect been erased by the authoritarian state of Eritrea. Asrat is one of 16 journalists who disappeared into Eritrea’s prison system 25 years ago on Black Tuesday – 18 September 2001 – when the government shut down all of the newspapers in the country.

stories.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bududa has suffered repeated deadly landslides over the years By Ondiro Oganga Â and Â Swaibu Ibrahim ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Kampala Published 19 November 2026 Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations. The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides. Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods. The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.

stories.title: Tours télécoms : le rachat du géant IHS par MTN franchit un cap décisif en zone Cemac
stories.summary: Selon nos informations, le régulateur de la Cemac a donné son feu vert sous conditions au rachat d’IHS par MTN. L’opérateur doit présenter un cahier des charges pour rassurer ses rivaux, notamment au Cameroun où l’enjeu est critique.

stories.summary: Au Cameroun, l’administration s’invite dans la bataille électorale À moins d’une semaine de la clôture du dépôt des candidatures, les accusations de blocages administratifs se multiplient. stories.title: Entre Émiratis et Saoudiens, Djibouti arbitre une nouvelle guerre du Golfe
stories.summary: Entre Émiratis et Saoudiens, Djibouti arbitre une nouvelle guerre du Golfe Abou Dhabi et Riyad cherchent depuis des années à conforter leurs positions dans la Corne de l’Afrique et placent Djibouti au cœur de leur stratégie. Décryptage d’un jeu d’influences, dans lequel l’arrivée annoncée d’Israël au Somaliland rebat les cartes. Le prince héritier saoudien, Mohammed Ben Salmane (MBS), aux côtés du président djiboutien, Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, à Djeddah, en marge du sommet de la Ligue arabe, le 19 mai 2023. © AFP Par Olivier Caslin (Envoyé spécial à Djibouti) Publié aujourd'hui à 07h00 Lecture : 5 minutes. stories.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
stories.summary: Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef View image in fullscreen Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report. In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday.

stories.title: Peine de mort en Afrique : du Nigeria au Burkina Faso, le continent face aux revirements
stories.summary: En vingt ans, le nombre de pays africains abolitionnistes a doublé. Mais, par ailleurs, le Burkina Faso vient de rétablir la peine capitale et des dizaines d’autres États la maintiennent sans l’appliquer. Aujourd’hui, où en est exactement l’abolition et qu’est-ce qui permet de la préserver ?

stories.title: Au Sénégal, l’examen de la loi de finances 2027 s’ouvre sur fond de purge au sein de Pastef
stories.summary: Alors que le marathon budgétaire commence à l’Assemblée nationale, le conflit entre Ousmane Sonko et Bassirou Diomaye Faye vient de franchir un nouveau palier après l’éviction du chef de l’État des rangs du parti de son ancien Premier ministre.

stories.title: Guerre au Soudan : « Beaucoup de familles marient leurs filles de force en pensant qu’un mari les protégera du viol »
stories.summary: Depuis le début de la guerre, en 2023, l’avocate soudanaise Tahani Abbas recueille des témoignages de femmes violées. Elle explique, dans un entretien au « Monde », pourquoi si peu d’entre elles témoignent, dans une société très conservatrice où les victimes sont parfois tuées pour sauver l’honneur familial.

stories.title: Mines : la stratégie XXL de la Côte d’Ivoire pour devenir le prochain eldorado africain
stories.summary: La Côte d’Ivoire veut faire des mines et de l’énergie le deuxième pilier de son économie. Un plan de 38 000 milliards de F CFA, en partie porté par le secteur privé, entend développer le secteur extractif et sa transformation locale.

stories.title: Régularisation de 300 000 sans-papiers : la proposition arrive devant les députés français
stories.summary: Portée par un jeune député socialiste, Paul Christophle, la proposition de loi a peu de chances d’être votée. Mais elle a au moins le mérite de faire entendre une autre voix sur l’immigration et de valoir à son promoteur un début de notoriété.

stories.title: Le Bénin réclame de nouvelles restitutions d’œuvres pillées par la France, dont une sculpture emblématique du dieu Gou
stories.summary: Le pays, qui a récupéré, en 2021, 26 biens culturels spoliés pendant la colonisation, demande le retour de 35 autres objets figurant dans les collections du Musée du quai Branly. La loi-cadre adoptée en mai par le Parlement français pourrait lui permettre de les obtenir d’ici à deux ans.

stories.title: Au Gabon, comment « l’affaire Dylan », un jeune blessé par balles, est devenue très politique
stories.summary: Au Gabon, comment « l’affaire Dylan », un jeune blessé par balles, est devenue très politique De l’arrestation de l’oncle d’Ali Bongo Ondimba à l’implication très personnelle de Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, l’hospitalisation d’un adolescent victime de tirs d’arme à feu a fait les gros titres à Libreville et relancé le débat sur l’indépendance de la justice. stories.title: À Rabat, l’émissaire américain Mike Waltz détaille les prochaines étapes prévues au Sahara occidental
stories.summary: À Rabat, l’émissaire américain Mike Waltz détaille les prochaines étapes prévues au Sahara occidental En tournée au Liban et au Maroc, le représentant américain auprès de l’ONU est venu confirmer le soutien de Washington au règlement du dossier du Sahara sous autonomie marocaine. Il a aussi mis en garde toutes les parties contre les risques d’une option militaire. Le représentant américain auprès de l’ONU, Michael Waltz, et le ministre marocain des Affaires étrangères, Nasser Bourita, à Rabat le 17 novembre 2026. © Facebook Maroc Diplomatie Par Jassim Ahdani (à Rabat) Publié aujourd'hui à 11h53 Lecture : 3 minutes. À l’issue de leur entretien, les deux responsables ont réaffirmé leur convergence sur la perspective d’un règlement du différend du Sahara occidental fondé sur l’autonomie sous souveraineté marocaine.

stories.title: Africa: The African Development Bank Group and JICA Explore New Avenues of Cooperation for Africa
stories.summary: The African Development Bank Group and JICA Explore New Avenues of Cooperation for Africa 17 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) The African Development Bank Group (Bank Group) and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) are looking to broaden their partnership in support of Africa's development, following talks between their leaders on 13 November. During an in-depth review ('deep dive') at JICA's headquarters, Bank Group President Dr Sidi Ould Tah and JICA President Dr Akihiko Tanaka first took stock of their cooperation across various sectors including agriculture and infrastructure, and then discussed new areas of opportunity. The two leaders were accompanied by their respective technical teams. Critical minerals, health, skills development, digital technology, artificial intelligence, resilience and crisis response were among the areas under consideration, alongside initiatives aimed at mobilising more private capital for Africa. Dr Ould Tah was keen to emphasise the potential of the partnership between the Bank Group and JICA to mobilise more private capital, promote access to technology and strengthen the engagement of Japanese businesses and investors in Africa.

stories.title: Au Tchad, le Comité d’autodéfense de Miski dénonce les attaques de drones de l’armée
stories.summary: Au Tchad, le Comité d’autodéfense de Miski dénonce les attaques de drones de l’armée Au moins une personne a été tuée ce 17 novembre par une frappe de drone dans le Tibesti, dans le nord-ouest du pays. Le Comité d’autodéfense de Miski l’attribue « au régime tchadien ». La région de Tibesti, frontalière de la Libye et du Niger. © MICHAEL RUNKEL / ROBERT HARDING RF / ROBERTHARDING VIA AFP Par Jeune Afrique Publié aujourd'hui à 10h22 Lecture : 2 minutes. Bilan provisoire : un mort civil », selon un communiqué de cette milice publié mardi sur sa page officielle.

stories.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
stories.summary: Smoke plumes rise on Myanmar’s side of border as Rohingya refugees walk on the shore after crossing the Bangladesh-Myanmar border by boat. Photograph: Danish Siddiqui/Reuters View image in fullscreen Smoke plumes rise on Myanmar’s side of border as Rohingya refugees walk on the shore after crossing the Bangladesh-Myanmar border by boat. Photograph: Danish Siddiqui/Reuters Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay , if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya. ‘They showed no mercy’: mapping the Rohingya villages being erased by rebel forces Read more The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017. It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention.

stories.title: Comment NSIA compte convertir sa forte croissance en rentabilité
stories.summary: Le pôle bancaire de NSIA s’est hissé à la cinquième place de l’UEMOA, devançant deux géants marocains. Propulsé par sa filiale ivoirienne, le groupe doit désormais relever le défi de la rentabilité.

stories.title: Entre le FC Barcelone et Kinshasa, l’impitoyable match des intermédiaires
stories.summary: Entre le FC Barcelone et Kinshasa, l’impitoyable match des intermédiaires Le partenariat entre le club de football catalan et la RDC devait promouvoir la destination congolaise. Il a déclenché une guerre entre deux apporteurs d’affaires français, Aurélien Logeais et Olivier Nsiabamfumu, qui se disputent plusieurs millions d’euros. Raphina du FC Barcelone joue lors du match de La Liga EA Sports 2025/26 opposant le FC Barcelone au Deportivo Alavés au stade Camp Nou de Barcelone, en Espagne, le 29 novembre 2025. © Gongora/NurPhoto via AFP Par Romain Chanson Publié aujourd'hui à 06h55 Lecture : 10 minutes. Le stade rénové du FC Barcelone est le théâtre d’un intense bras de fer entre deux intermédiaires français qui revendiquent la paternité du projet de sponsoring entre le club de football catalan et le gouvernement congolais .

stories.title: Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito By Akisa Wandera BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lobito Published 18 November 2026 As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments. She is thinking about getting around more easily. The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast. For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient. "Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.

stories.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
stories.summary: Ursula von der Leyen and Abdel Fatah al-Sisi after a meeting in Cairo in March 2024. Photograph: Stavros Ioannides/PIO/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Ursula von der Leyen and Abdel Fatah al-Sisi after a meeting in Cairo in March 2024. Photograph: Stavros Ioannides/PIO/AFP/Getty Images European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi. The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen , the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

stories.title: En RDC, Ebola tue massivement les enfants : « Je ne peux même pas le prendre dans mes bras pour le réconforter »
stories.summary: Près des trois quarts des moins de 5 ans contaminés par la maladie à virus Ebola n’y survivent pas. A Bunia et Beni, épicentres de l’épidémie, les deuils s’enchaînent, tandis que plus de 2 280 enfants se retrouvent orphelins.

stories.title: Africa: From Dependency to Sovereignty - What the International Conference On Public Health in Africa 2026 Must Deliver for Africa's Health Security
stories.summary: From Dependency to Sovereignty - What the International Conference On Public Health in Africa 2026 Must Deliver for Africa's Health Security 17 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) In late November 2026, Addis Ababa will host the 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), co-convened by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the Government of Ethiopia. Its theme, 'Africa's Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from health dependency and vulnerability to ownership and resilience', states its intent. It is also a response to a financing and epidemiological reality that no longer allows business as usual. External health aid to Africa was projected to fall by about 70% between 2021 and 2025, while African countries were expected to spend $81 billion United States dollars (USD) (on debt service in 2025 alone). Twenty-four years after the Abuja Declaration, only three countries, Botswana, Cabo Verde and Rwanda, have achieved the agreed target of 15% of national budgets allocated to health, and 30 African Union (AU) Member States allocate less than 10%.

stories.title: Congo Ebola Outbreak: How Fear and Mistrust Drive Community Spread
stories.summary: As the Ebola virus spreads in eastern Congo, health teams struggle to curb fatal delays in seeking medical care and the widespread desire to treat sick relatives at home.

stories.title: L’arrêt très attendu de la Cour internationale de justice sur la question du génocide des Rohingya
stories.summary: La CIJ dira, jeudi 19 novembre, si la Birmanie a commis un génocide contre la minorité musulmane. Alors que la décision devrait préciser les contours de la définition juridique de « génocide », les tentatives d’intimidation américaines contre les juges se multiplient.

stories.title: De Fela Kuti à Burna Boy, les radios de « GTA » racontent l’ascension des musiques nigérianes et sud-africaines
stories.summary: Dix-huit ans après avoir glissé des titres du père de l’afrobeat, le Nigérian Fela Kuti, dans le jeu vidéo « Grand Theft Auto IV », « GTA VI », qui sort jeudi 19 novembre, confie au chanteur nigérian Burna Boy une station entière consacrée aux musiques du Nigeria, d’Afrique du Sud et du Ghana.

stories.title: Compromis à la francophonie, Bassirou Faye radié du Pastef, CAN 2027 : l'hebdo Afrique
stories.summary: Publicité Récap Compromis à la francophonie, Bassirou Faye radié du Pastef, CAN 2027 : l'hebdo Afrique Publié le : 20/11/2026 - 09:09 7 min Temps de lecture Partager Par : FRANCE 24 La secrétaire générale de la Francophonie, Louise Mushikiwabo, écoute les délégués lors de la cérémonie de clôture du 20e Sommet de la Francophonie, à Phnom Penh, au Cambodge, le 16 novembre 2026. © Soveit Yarn, Reuters Le Pastef, parti majoritaire au Sénégal dirigé par le président de l'Assemblée nationale Ousmane Sonko , a officialisé mardi le départ de ses rangs du président Bassirou Diomaye Faye , en conflit avec son ancien Premier ministre, en pleine crise budgétaire entre l'exécutif et le Parlement. Une analyse de David Rich à lire sur France 24 . Près de 700 000 personnes ont été déplacées par des affrontements entre forces armées des régions Somali et de l'Oromia, qui font rage depuis près d'un mois dans le sud de l' Éthiopie , a annoncé jeudi l'ONG britannique Islamic Relief. Les premiers combats remontent à fin octobre, après qu'un drapeau de la région Somali a été hissé à Moyale, ville éthiopienne frontalière avec le Kenya , administrée conjointement par les deux régions éthiopiennes. Deux vaccins ciblant spécifiquement la souche d'Ebola qui sévit en République démocratique du Congo devraient faire l'objet d'essais cliniques sur place dès la semaine prochaine, a annoncé mardi l'Organisation mondiale de la santé.

stories.title: Ndeye Dieynaba Ndiaye, chercheuse : « Il est temps pour l’Afrique de se doter d’une politique migratoire commune »
stories.summary: La spécialiste des mobilités et du droit des réfugiés décrypte, dans un entretien au « Monde », les logiques à l’œuvre derrière l’accord passé, lundi 16 novembre à Vienne, entre cinq pays européens et le Rwanda, permettant de renvoyer dans ce pays des demandeurs d’asile déboutés.

stories.title: Chaos as crackdown on illegal mining in Guinea causes wave of regional displacement
stories.summary: Artisanal gold miners in Kanadjiguilla, Mali, clamber on to a repatriation vehicle bound for Burkina Faso. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Artisanal gold miners in Kanadjiguilla, Mali, clamber on to a repatriation vehicle bound for Burkina Faso. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Chaos as crackdown on illegal mining in Guinea causes wave of regional displacement Ban on illegal artisanal mining triggers mass exodus and diplomatic tensions with neighbouring Sahel states In the border town of Kourémalé, split between Guinea and Mali, thousands of families have been trudging across the frontier over the past week after a sudden ban on illegal artisanal mining triggered a wave of displacement and a regional diplomatic dispute. Some, like Seydou Traore, a miner in his 30s from Burkina Faso , made the 78-mile trek from Kourémalé to Ouezzindougou, farther inward. Last week, he gathered a small bundle of his belongings and fled Guinea after security forces ordered him and fellow miners to leave. “We worked hard there, honestly,” he told Agence France-Presse (AFP). “Then one day everything changed.

stories.title: Génocide des Tutsi : devant la cour d’assises de Paris, le procès du Rwandais Madjaliwa Safari et des tueries aux « barrières »
stories.summary: Arrêté à Tours en 2023, le commerçant de 61 ans est poursuivi pour les faits imprescriptibles de « génocide » et de « crimes contre l’humanité ». D’après plusieurs témoins, il aurait ordonné des meurtres et participé à des massacres de Tutsi en 1994.

stories.title: ‘I’m not ready to go to jail’: co-founder of Egypt’s last independent media outlet faces prison
stories.summary: Lina Attalah, editor in chief of the Cairo-based Mada Masr, will be in court this week on charges of ‘publishing false news’. Photograph: K Desouki/AFP/Getty View image in fullscreen Lina Attalah, editor in chief of the Cairo-based Mada Masr, will be in court this week on charges of ‘publishing false news’. Photograph: K Desouki/AFP/Getty ‘I’m not ready to go to jail’: co-founder of Egypt’s last independent media outlet faces prison Mada Masr, the news site co-founded by Lina Attalah just before the 2013 military coup, is fighting for its life after being shut down, but its journalists have not given up hope F acing a year in prison for running Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr , Lina Attalah is trying to focus on the everyday: waking at dawn to hear the birds sing before Cairo’s streets come alive and visiting Mada Masr’s shuttered offices with her reporters to water the plants and feed their four cats. Attalah is the reluctant face of Egypt’s embattled independent press at a moment of crisis. In the last six weeks, Egyptian authorities have waged a renewed crackdown on the few remaining independent media outlets left in the country, beginning with the arrest of the entire newsroom of the factchecking website Matsadaash.

stories.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
stories.summary: The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters View image in fullscreen The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”. The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country. In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

stories.title: BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West Africa
stories.summary: Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBC Image caption, Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing housework By Madina Maishanu BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Goronyo Published 17 November 2026 As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school. "Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says. One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village. "They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says. Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home.

stories.title: Le XXᵉ Sommet de la francophonie paralysé par les tensions diplomatiques​

All photographs by Kenneth Zindondo ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles T he mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika .

stories.title: Town rebuilt after devastating floods becomes showcase for Libyan strongman's rule
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Whole areas of Derna have been entirely rebuilt By Tim Whewell Reporting from Derna Published 16 November 2026 "It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna. Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him. Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya. It is part of a rapid $2bn (Â£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.

stories.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
stories.summary: Image source, Braton Serge/BBC By Ruth Alonga BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Butembo Published 15 November 2026 When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified. They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there. "Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him. But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive. This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern.

stories.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PRq5 Prefer DW on Google Nigeria's 2027 general election will take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformation Image: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis . He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi. The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI) . Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died. The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election.

stories.title: Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians Composite: Guardian Design / Getty Images Strikes with huge death tolls are an increasing occurrence as UAVs ‘bring the war to places that were once safe’ The first drone struck the busy transport hub near a market in Al-Dibab as hundreds of people gathered to board trucks to take them back to their homes. Ten minutes later on the evening of 18 October, a second drone hit the same site in the town in West Kordofan state, Sudan . At least 139 people were killed. Eight days after the “double-tap” attack – designed to maximise casualties by killing and injuring emergency responders, volunteers and bystanders on top of the original victims – a drone hit a busy market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur. Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in Sudan, put the death toll from that attack at 103. “I lost my 19-year-old son,” a Nyala resident told Agence France-Presse. “We buried him alongside more than 70 bodies in a single site.” View image in fullscreen The remains of Alneam market after a drone strike in the disputed Abyei region along the border between South Sudan and Sudan last month.

stories.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
stories.summary: Image source, Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) Image caption, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba has signalled his intention to run for president in the next elections By Wycliffe Muia Published 14 November 2026 In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief. Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks. The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades. Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party. This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.
